text: **Privacy and security are neighbors, not twins.** Security is about stopping harm to systems and data. Privacy is about how personal information is gathered, used, and shared. The exam treats that split as something you should be able to explain.

**Sorting likelihood and impact into rough bands, rather than dollars, is the qualitative style.** Numeric estimates of chance and loss are the other style. This exam stays with the bands. The numeric version shows up on later certs such as CASP+ and CISSP.

**You will not be asked to configure a product from this chapter.** You still need the controls well enough to read a log, suggest a fix, and recognize the tool when a scenario names it. The test assumes that everyday familiarity.

**This topic is named in the objectives, so it is fair game.** The point is fewer one-off analyst steps: write the work down the same way every time, then pull separate tools into one monitoring view.
**Serverless, virtual machines, and containers are named on the outline.** For each, be ready to say what you gain, what you still have to secure, and a situation where you would choose it.
**Config-file locations are on the outline.** Know the usual Windows and Linux places. macOS paths are rarely the thing being asked.

**The OS list for this objective is short and specific.** What the Registry is, what hardening removes or locks, where configs live, which processes belong to the OS, and why CPU architecture changes the malware and tools you will see.

**Be able to contrast on-prem, cloud, and hybrid**, including what each does to your control and visibility. Segmentation keeps different risk levels apart. Zero trust, SASE, and software-defined networking are the design ideas this exam uses for modern networks.
**SSO is on the outline without product names.** Know what one login for many apps buys you, and how much breaks if that single login is stolen.

**Federation is named, not spelled out.** It means trusting another party to say who a user is. Know why you would do that, the trust problem it creates, and the usual protocol names at a glance: SAML, OAuth, and OpenID.

**The network clues on the outline are concrete:** spikes, beaconing, scans, bandwidth that does not fit, devices nobody owns, odd peer-to-peer flows, and sessions on ports that should be closed. None of that is visible until you can capture the traffic.

**A full disk or a traffic spike is not automatically an intrusion.** Practice telling a real compromise signal apart from a busy but normal day. Objective 1.4 treats indicators as an intel idea; here you are learning to spot the behavior.

**Traffic on a port you did not expect is usually one of two stories:** someone is probing, or an attacker stood up a new service. Do not stop at the port number. Look for context that says which story you are in.
**For network clues, the exam wants three things:** what the malicious pattern looks like, how you would notice it, and how you would decide it is an attack rather than new but legitimate traffic.

**In this spot the outline avoids the word malware.** It says malicious processes, and software nobody approved. Use those labels in an answer. Viruses and other malware names usually describe the same situation.

**On the outline the persistence item is scheduled tasks.** That is the Windows term. cron is the matching feature on Unix, Linux, and macOS, so a scenario that mentions cron is asking about the same idea.
**Social engineering and disguised links sit in the leftover bucket of this objective.** They are still common. Phishing often hides the real destination behind a messy or encoded link.

**These application clues are directly testable.** Activity outside the app's normal pattern is often the first sign, caught in logs, file-integrity checks, or by a person who notices. A new account, especially an admin one, is a common compromise mark, and app-level account creation may never hit a central log, so tie admin accounts to change approval. Strange output can be garbage data or errors, and desktop apps are harder to watch centrally than a server or API. Outbound surprises include check-ins to a controller, files leaving, and the host attacking others, so watch egress. A stopped service might be a crash, a flood, or a compromised app, so watch both process state and what users feel. Logs only help if you know where they live and what a bad line looks like.

**This outline does not name a required log format.** Older versions did. You should still practice a few common logs, because deciding whether something is malicious means reading whatever log you are handed.
**The exam will not score you on one vendor's error codes.** Practice reading an unfamiliar log by pulling out time, host, action, and result instead of memorizing a product's layout.
**Email analysis on the outline covers two jobs:** how you inspect a message, and the controls that strain out spam and phishing. Study both.
**You do not need to author Python or PowerShell.** You do need to tell which language a snippet is, and roughly what it is doing.
**Regex mastery is not required.** Know that a pattern can match a whole class of strings, and be able to read a simple expression.
**Judge a threat feed on three questions:** did it arrive in time, does it apply to you, and is it accurate? Be ready to say why each one matters.
**Shared intel shows up in five places on this exam:** during an incident, while handling vulnerabilities, in risk decisions, when engineers design controls, and in detection and monitoring.
**STIX and TAXII are how a lot of real intel is packaged and moved.** They are not named on the outline, so do not expect a direct question, but you will meet them in the job.

**Open-source collection is a habit, not one website.** Practice pulling leads from CSIRT writeups, government advisories, public social posts, discussion forums, and places on the dark web where criminals trade notes.
**Insiders are split into people who mean harm and people who do not.** Answer with that split. Script kiddies and supply-chain actors were added on this version of the outline.
**Asset discovery here centers on scans such as nmap and on fingerprinting.** Connect those techniques to finding a host, naming it, and putting it on an inventory.
**Active collection touches the host. Passive collection only watches.** Passive work infers from traffic or published data and does not probe. The outline asks for that difference.

**Before exam day, be able to find and read five log families:** system events, firewall, web application firewall, proxy, and intrusion detection or prevention. Later chapters go deeper. The skill is the same.

**Ignore the outline's tool buckets and remember the job each one does.** nmap is the port scanner worth real practice. Angry IP Scanner also finds open ports, and it is the quicker, simpler cousin. Recon-ng and Maltego both work from public information; Maltego is the one that draws relationships. Metasploit wraps scanning together with exploit and testing modules. If time is short, put it into nmap and Metasploit.

**Four frameworks show up often enough to mix up.** PCI DSS is the card-brand rule set, CIS is a benchmark collection, OWASP focuses on application security, and the ISO 27000 family is a management-system standard. Know which problem each one is trying to solve.

**In vulnerability scanning, active means the scanner talks to hosts.** It walks addresses and looks for open ports and weak apps, and it is noisy. Passive means watching packets for signs of old software. Do not confuse this pair with the recon definitions on the previous pages.
**Separate these scan pairs:** logged in versus not, an agent on the host versus none, and scanning from inside versus from the internet.
**Repeating scans only help if the first snapshot exists.** Take a baseline, then later runs show what got fixed and what newly appeared.
**Cloud-provider consoles are out of scope.** The open-source names to recognize are Pacu, Prowler, and Scout Suite.
**Expect to be shown scanner output, including from a web-app scanner, and asked to name the issue.** Practice reading those reports until the finding is obvious.

**CVSS publishes a severity number from 0 through 10.** Be able to decode the base fields: how the attacker reaches the bug, how fiddly the exploit is, what rights they already need, whether a person has to click, whether the impact crosses a security boundary, and how badly confidentiality, integrity, and availability suffer.
**Validating a report means sorting each item into one of four bins:** a real flaw the tool caught, a real flaw it missed, a clean host it correctly cleared, or an alarm that is not actually a flaw.
**An integer overflow is the arithmetic cousin of a buffer overflow.** The math result is a whole number too big for the variable that is supposed to hold it.

**Stack and heap are different targets.** The stack holds local values and return addresses and the operating system manages it. The heap holds objects the program creates, and the developer manages that memory.
**Injection is not only SQL.** The same trick appears when user input is dropped into XML or into an LDAP lookup.

**The outline lists the cross-site scripting variants separately.** Know which one stores the payload on the server, which one bounces it back in a response, and which one runs in the page's DOM without a server round trip.
**Scenario questions here want a control that matches the flaw.** A definition recited back is not the answer they are grading.
**How bad a risk is comes from two inputs:** how likely it is, and how large the damage would be. Keep both, not one.

**Four responses to risk.** Reduce it, stop the activity that creates it, live with it on purpose, or shift it (often with insurance or a contract). Be ready with an example of each, and to name which one a scenario is using.

**The secure-coding habits named in the objectives are testable, not background.** That includes checking input, encoding output, parameterized queries, session and authentication handling, and protecting the data itself.
**Static analysis reads the code without running it. Dynamic analysis runs it.** Fuzzing is named on the outline: feed the program messy input and see what breaks. Know how those differ.
**Forensics, root-cause work, and lessons learned sit after the incident is handled.** They are not the step where you stop the spread.

**Incident response sits next to continuity and disaster recovery, and the teams should plan together.** Continuity tries to keep core work going during a disruption. Disaster recovery tries to get normal operations back after they stop. An incident can set either one off.
**A playbook is a recipe for one incident type.** Follow it, but it does not replace judgment. A skilled responder may step off the recipe when the facts do not match.

**Criticality goes up when the data itself is sensitive.** Be ready to recognize health records, payment and finance data, intellectual property, personal identifiers, other sensitive personal details, crown-jewel systems, and ordinary internal company files. The architecture chapter spends more time on those categories.
**Three named models are in scope: MITRE ATT&CK, the Diamond Model, and the kill chain.** Know the job each model does. A title by itself will not answer the question.

**You do not need to run a giant indicator platform for the exam.** Free feeds such as OTX hold tens of millions of clues. For the test, know what an indicator is and how you would spot one in a log or a short scenario.

**Evidence handling on this exam means four ideas:** who had it (chain of custody), whether the copy still matches (integrity), keeping it from being changed or deleted (preservation), and a legal hold when a case may need it.
**Box the incident in before you clean it up.** Stopping the spread comes ahead of wiping the damage or restoring data.
**An indicator of compromise is a concrete clue that a breach already happened.** Examples: an address, a file hash, traffic that does not fit the baseline, or a privileged account behaving oddly.
**Vulnerability reports the exam cares about name the flaw, the hosts, a risk score, a way to mitigate, whether it keeps coming back, and what to fix first.**
**Be able to name the metric groups used to judge a vulnerability program, and the reasons a fix stalls.** You should recognize those blockers in a scenario and say why they hurt.

**The outline puts the weight on stopping the spread, cleaning the environment, and restoring service.** The forensics material is the surrounding skill. As you go, it keeps asking how wide the event spread, how bad it was, and why it was possible.
**Hashing sits on objective 1.3.** Be ready to explain a hash used to name a file, or to show that a copy still matches the original.
**Two products you should be able to pull out of a forensic effort:** why it happened, and what the team would do differently next time.

**Walk into questions from this section able to talk about three evidence ideas:** who has held an item, how you keep it from being altered or thrown away, and when lawyers require you to freeze deletion.

**Three goals keep showing up.** Keep secrets from people who should not see them. Stop quiet edits to data or systems, whether the edit was deliberate or a mistake. Make sure the service is actually up when someone who is allowed to use it needs it.
**A risk needs both a weakness and something that might use it.** The weakness can be in a device, app, or process. The threat is the force, person, or event that could take advantage of it.

**Sort threats into four piles.** Someone is trying to hurt you. A person doing their job makes a mistake. Equipment, software, or a control fails because it is worn out, overloaded, or past its capacity. A disaster, natural or human-made, lands from outside the organization's control.

**Three network controls do different jobs.** Network access control decides who gets on and can demand that the device meet a baseline. A firewall sits on a boundary. Segmentation isolates networks that should not share the same trust.

**Endpoints get safer in four practical ways.** Turn off what you do not need and lock the settings, preferably from one place. Patch the OS and the apps so known holes close. Group Policy pushes those settings to many Windows machines at once. Endpoint security software watches for malware and similar threats.

**A penetration test shows the network the way an attacker would.** NIST's flow is plan, discover, attack, then report. The useful output is a list of holes someone could actually use, which makes it a planning tool and not just a stunt.

**Reverse engineering tries to learn how hardware or software works on the inside.** A sandbox catches bad software by what it does, not by a signature. Other reverse-engineering work is slow, difficult, and often fails.

**Machine learning is the part of future analytics with the most promise.** Security tools already throw off more data than a person can read. Models pull patterns out of that pile, often using what the product has already learned from other customers.
**Analyst work is slow and easy to get wrong.** Written processes, fewer manual steps, and tools that actually connect to each other make people faster and cut mistakes.
**Serverless, virtual machines, and containers.** For each one, know a typical use, the reason you would choose it, and what sets it apart from the other two.

**Operating-system security in one list.** What hardening is and why it matters. What the Registry is and why it matters. Where Windows and Linux keep configuration. What a core system process is. Why CPU architecture changes which attacks and tools apply.
**Logs fall apart if the clocks disagree.** Time sync, usually NTP, is what lines them up. The log level decides how much detail you keep, so pick it on purpose.

**Compare network designs.** What changes about security when the stack is on-prem, in the cloud, or split across both. Why you separate segments, and how. What SASE, zero trust, and software-defined networking are each trying to accomplish.

**Identity pieces to be able to explain.** More than one factor, and what the factor types are. Login without a password. One sign-on for many apps, and why a company wants that. Federation, where another party asserts identity. Privileged-access management for powerful accounts. A cloud access security broker in front of cloud apps.

**Encryption and sensitive data.** The usual pieces of a public key infrastructure. Why you inspect TLS and what you give up when you do. What data-loss prevention needs in order to work. Personal data is about a person; cardholder data is about the payment card.

**Network malice has a recognizable shape.** Heavy bandwidth use, beaconing, strange peer-to-peer, scans and sweeps, spikes, traffic you did not expect, activity on odd ports, and devices that should not be on the network. Know how bandwidth ties into spotting those events.

**Host clues live in resource use and in changes.** Watch CPU, memory, and disk, and know what a surprise spike can mean. Look for software that should not be installed, file and Registry changes, privilege changes, and bad processes. Built-in tools can find a lot of this. Data leaving the host is its own pattern. Scheduled tasks are a place persistence hides.

**Application clues:** behavior that does not match the app, brand-new accounts, rights that do not fit the job, output that does not make sense, connections the app should not make, and a service that drops. Logs and monitoring are how you see the outage.

**Tools, and what each one is for.** Wireshark and tcpdump for packets, and be able to read both. SIEM, SOAR, and EDR are not the same product. DNS and IP reputation, Whois, and abuse lists such as AbuseIPDB. File checks with strings and VirusTotal. Sandboxes such as Joe Sandbox and Cuckoo, plus the general idea of running a sample somewhere safe.

**Techniques, not just tools.** Spot command-and-control patterns, especially a regular check-in. Read suspicious Windows and Linux commands. Inspect mail headers, know why an embedded link is dangerous, and know what SPF, DKIM, and DMARC each prove. Hash files. Watch accounts for behavior that cannot be real, such as travel that is physically impossible.

**Languages and formats you should be able to skim.** JSON and XML. Python, PowerShell, and a Linux shell script, well enough to say what the snippet does. Simple regular expressions for searching files or data.

**Actor labels to keep straight:** an advanced persistent threat, a nation-state, a hacktivist, organized crime, a script kiddie, an insider who means it, and an insider who does not. Supply chain belongs on the list because a vendor can be the way in.

**Tactics, techniques, and procedures are three altitudes.** Tactics are the strategy. Techniques are the tools and methods, technical or not, used to get in, stay in, and take something. Procedures are the order those techniques get chained together.

**Some intel is public and some is paid or private.** Public leads come from dark-web markets, CSIRT and CERT posts, government advisories, forums, blogs, and social media. Sharing groups are often built around one industry. Judge a source by freshness, fit for your environment, and track record, and be ready to say how sure you are.

**Hunting and indicators.** Know how indicators are gathered, studied, and then used. Hunters look hard at configuration and misconfiguration. An isolated network lets you watch an attack without it touching production. Prioritize assets the business cannot lose. A honeypot is one active-defense example.

**Active recon probes the target, and it is how you build a map.** A port scan is a usual first move. nmap is the common tool for hosts, ports, OS guesses, and services. Replies also reveal topology. Knowing which port belongs with which service makes the results readable.
**Passive discovery never pokes the target.** Logs, config files, DNS, and Whois already hold a lot. A packet capture shows what is on the wire and can also record what an active scan did.

**Read output, not just names.** nmap and Angry IP Scanner both find assets. Recon-ng and Maltego both organize public intel and recon notes. Metasploit gathers information and also runs exploits. Know the job of each one, and what a basic result looks like.

**Discovery should tell you which machines exist, what they run, which services they expose, and how they are wired together.** Scans that map the network, OS and service guesses (including the ones that are wrong), and clues such as time-to-live all feed that picture.
**Some scans are required from outside the company, and some are required by your own rules.** PCI DSS and FISMA are the outside examples. An internal security policy is the inside example.

**A discovery scan builds the inventory. Then you choose targets.** Use how sensitive the data is, how exposed the system is, which services it runs, and whether it is test, development, or production.

**Daily, weekly, or monthly is a business choice.** It depends on how much risk you will tolerate, what regulations say, license limits, and what operations can stand. Some teams drop the calendar and watch continuously.

**A scan is tunable.** Change how aggressive it is, turn checks on or off, and add a logged-in scan or a host agent on top of a basic network pass. Looking from more than one place, inside and outside, shows different holes.
**Two upkeep jobs for the scanner itself.** Update the scanner software so it stays safe and gains features. Update the check plugins so the findings match current flaws.

**The fix path should be mostly automatic and should land in the ticketing you already use.** After a repair, test that it worked, then close the item. The vulnerability system should also report and alert, not only list findings.
**You cannot repair everything today, so rank the work.** Use how important the system and the data are, how hard the fix is, how severe the flaw is, and how exposed the host is.
**Other teams push back on scans for predictable reasons.** The scan can slow a service. A contract or uptime promise may forbid the outage. Change control may have to approve the window.

**A useful scan report does more than name a flaw.** Expect a severity, the exchange that set the alarm off (what was sent and what came back), and a suggested repair. Confirming the hit and getting it fixed are still your job.

**The CVSS base score is a 0-to-10 summary.** It folds in how an attacker reaches the flaw, how hard the exploit is, what privileges they need, and how badly confidentiality, integrity, and availability are hurt.

**A lot of findings come from servers and user devices.** Unpatched software and operating systems that are past support are the frequent, easy wins. Buffer overflows, privilege escalation, and running attacker-supplied code usually come from application bugs. Protocols that should have been retired show up often too.

**Phones and operational technology are harder to scan than a server.** So are vehicles, drones, building automation, door-control systems, and industrial controls. Know that those scans need a different level of care, and be able to read the results.

**Code flaws need the analyst and the developer in the same conversation.** Web apps are where SQL and XML injection show up. Any software can have a buffer, integer, or heap overflow. The repair is often a code change plus another scan to prove it took.

**Know the application-attack menu well enough to recognize it.** Cross-site scripting, overflows, poisoned training or input data, broken access control, weak or misused cryptography, injection, forged requests, and the other usual code flaws. Knowing the method is how you pick a defense and spot the attack.

**Find the risks, then rank them.** A business impact look estimates how likely each one is and how large the effect would be. That ranking is how you tell the rest of the company what to worry about first.
**Vendors bring risk your own assessment will not see.** Checking the supply chain reduces surprises. Hardware-authenticity checks look for tampering after the device left the vendor.

**Four strategies, in plain terms.** Avoidance changes the business so the risk is gone. Mitigation lowers the chance or the damage. Transfer moves some of it to someone else. Acceptance means you keep operating and own the risk on purpose.

**Code-testing tools split by whether the program runs.** Static review inspects structure and content without executing it. Dynamic review executes it. Fuzzing is a dynamic method that throws generated input at the program. A debugger lets you step through a compiled program when you do not have the original source.

**Documents in the policy stack do different jobs.** A policy is management's intent, short and high level. A standard is the mandatory detail. A procedure is the steps. Those three are required. A guideline is optional advice. Some frameworks prescribe controls. Others start from risk and let you choose.

**A typical policy set, not a mandatory checklist.** Information security, acceptable use, who owns data, how long data is kept, how accounts are managed, and passwords. Which ones you publish depends on the business.
**An exception needs a process, not a shrug.** Say what is being skipped, who can approve it, and which extra control covers the gap you just opened.

**Event, security event, incident.** An event is anything you can observe. A security event is an observation tied to a security function. An incident means policy, acceptable use, or ordinary secure practice was broken, or is about to be. Incidents are built from events. Most events never become one.

**Four phases, and they loop.** Prepare. Detect and analyze. Contain, eradicate, and recover. Then the work after the incident. You go back to an earlier phase when new facts show up. It is not a straight line.

**Clues arrive from four directions.** Alerts from intrusion detection or prevention, the SIEM, antivirus, file-integrity tools, and outside monitoring. Logs from the OS, services, apps, network devices, and flows. Public news of new flaws and exploits. People, inside or outside, who report something odd.

**Policy, procedure, playbook.** The incident policy is the authority and the high-level direction. Procedures are the tactical detail the team needs. A playbook is the procedure for one kind of incident.

**The core team is responders. The wider team is everyone else the incident touches.** That can include specialists, IT support, legal, HR, and communications. They also coordinate with executives, police, and regulators.

**Incidents are often labeled by how they arrived.** Email, the web, someone pretending to be a trusted person, removable media, brute force or a flood, misuse by an insider, lost or stolen gear, or a path you never identified.
**Severity is more than one number.** How badly work is impaired. How much money is lost. How long services stay down and how hard they are to bring back. How sensitive the data involved is.

**Models are how you describe an attack the same way twice and notice the pieces you skipped.** Know Diamond, ATT&CK, and Lockheed Martin's kill chain. ATT&CK is also a vocabulary other tools already speak. OSSTMM and OWASP's testing guide are for planning how you will test against those attacks.

**A working indicator list.** Odd traffic and peer-to-peer you did not expect. Ports or addresses that do not belong. Someone pulling far more from a database or a file share than usual. Suspicious edits to files, the Registry, or configs. Usage that does not look human. Logins and privilege use that are wrong for the place or the hour. Floods, and DNS that does not fit.

**For each indicator family, know an example, how you would use it, and which log would show it.** The families are DNS, account behavior, resource use, file and config changes, privilege use, traffic, and floods.

**You keep evidence for incidents, internal investigations, and lawsuits.** A legal hold can pause ordinary deletion, or you may need an independent copy that someone else can verify. Write down custody when police or a court may be involved, and whenever a case might become legal later.
**Know common logs well enough to say whether a line is an incident or ordinary work.**

**Once you think an incident is underway, contain it.** Pick the move that fits the incident and the business impact. Typical moves: cut the network into segments, isolate the host, or take it off the network.

**A lot of evidence vanishes if you wait.** Memory and live connections will not be there later. Decide how important collection is while you are containing the incident, then handle what you take so a court could use it: preserve it, record who had it, and check that it still matches.
**Naming the attacker often burns time and ends nowhere.** The responder's job is the business. Police have a different goal. Know when those goals pull in opposite directions.
**After the incident is boxed in, remove every trace and get operations back.** Before you close it, check that the security controls are actually in place.

**Afterward, review the whole response and change the plan if you need to, through change control.** Write a summary that will still make sense later. Also decide what evidence to keep, which indicators to record, and what to keep watching.

**A vulnerability report usually carries the CVE, the score, a name, a description, the hosts, ways to mitigate, whether it has come back, and a priority.** Send it to the right people on a schedule. Compliance reports are a special case. The action plan after that can include configuration changes, patches, compensating controls, training, and notes about what the business requires.

**Metrics that actually steer a vulnerability program.** Trends show whether you are improving or a new problem is becoming normal. A top-ten list shows what is common. A critical list shows what is dangerous. Zero-days are hard to count, and leadership may still want them. A service target says how fast a fix should land, and whether you are hitting it.

**Why a fix stalls.** A contract that punishes downtime. Governance that adds delay. Fear that a patch will break a business process. Legacy or proprietary systems that have no patch, or that lose support if you apply one.
**Name the people who must hear about an incident, and include them when you declare and escalate.** That can mean legal, customers, the media, regulators, and law enforcement.

**Lead an incident report with a short summary a busy reader can finish.** Then cover the people involved, the action, the time, the place, and the reason. Add how bad it was, how far it spread, a timeline, what you would change, and the evidence you kept. Explaining the underlying cause is what keeps the next incident from being the same surprise.
**Time-to-detect, time-to-respond, and time-to-remediate tell you whether the response program works.** A raw count of alerts is a weaker signal, even when a manager asks for it.

**Evidence work you should be able to explain.** Why you collect it and how. Why custody has to be written down and kept intact. What a legal hold and preservation are, and when they apply. Which tools and steps let you collect and study data without wrecking it.

**A forensic case has a shape:** decide the scope, find where the data lives, plan, acquire, analyze, report. Usual targets include system details, file times, and access. Acquisition must not change the source. Use a write blocker, and hash the copy so you can show it still matches.
**Forensic work can sit inside the incident, not off to the side.** After you understand the event, write down why it was possible and what the team will change next time.
